item.title: #1 [0/100] Curative-intent management of de novo metastatic nasopharyngeal carcinoma: an evidence-based consensus guideline from the International Collaborating Oncology Organisations.
item.dc:creator: Guo QJ, Liu Q, Bossi P, Bonomo P, Colevas AD, Lee NY, Lu TZ, Lee V, Mehanna H, Ng WT, et al.

Authors: Guo QJ, Liu Q, Bossi P, Bonomo P, Colevas AD, Lee NY, Lu TZ, Lee V, Mehanna H, Ng WT, et al.
Journal: The Lancet. Oncology | DOI: 10.1016/S1470-2045(26)00347-5
Published: 2026-Nov-01
PMID: 42933448



Abstract:
Patients with de novo metastatic nasopharyngeal carcinoma were historically deemed incurable and treated with palliative intent. Emergence of potent systemic therapy in combination with local treatment for both locoregional and metastatic diseases has enabled long-term survival in some patients. This international guideline was developed through consensus-building by 54 experts from 46 centres across 18 countries or regions and endorsed by 17 oncology organisations. 32 recommendations across seven clinical domains were formulated, including 29 strong (≥80% agreement [consensus] or high quality of evidence) and three conditional recommendations (67-79% agreement). We recommend that curative-intent treatment should be offered to medically fit patients with no more than three metastatic lesions in two or fewer organs at baseline or following response to systemic therapy; multimodality treatment (comprising immunochemotherapy, locoregional radiotherapy, metastasis-directed therapy, and maintenance therapy) is recommended. This guideline provides a practical framework for standardisation of clinical management of de novo metastatic nasopharyngeal carcinoma and identification of key evidence gaps for future research.

item.title: #2 [0/100] Neoadjuvant short-course radiotherapy followed by camrelizumab and chemotherapy versus standard of care for locally advanced rectal cancer (UNION): a prespecified interim analysis of a multicentre, open-label, randomised, phase 3 trial.

Authors: Tao K, Lin Z, Zhang P, Chi P, Xiao Y, Hou Z, Xu X, Zhang A, Qiu X, Wu J, et al.
Journal: The Lancet. Oncology | DOI: 10.1016/S1470-2045(26)00446-8
Published: 2026-Nov-01
PMID: 42927765



Abstract:
BACKGROUND: To our knowledge, UNION is the first phase 3 trial to assess a neoadjuvant strategy incorporating radiotherapy, immunotherapy, and chemotherapy compared with standard care in patients with locally advanced rectal cancer, which reported positive results for the primary endpoint (blinded independent review committee [BIRC]-assessed pathological complete response rate; 39·8% vs 15·3%). Here, we present a prespecified interim analysis of event-free survival. METHODS: This open-label, randomised, phase 3 trial was conducted at nine hospitals in China. Eligible patients were aged 18-75 years with untreated cT3-4 or N+ rectal adenocarcinoma (≤10 cm distance from the anal verge) and an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status of 0 or 1. Patients were randomly assigned (1:1; stratified by clinical T stage and N stage), using permuted blocks, to receive neoadjuvant short-course radiotherapy (25 Gy in five fractions) followed by two cycles of intravenous camrelizumab (200 mg on day 1) plus CAPOX (oral capecitabine 1000 mg/m2 twice daily on days 1-14 and intravenous oxaliplatin 130 mg/m2 on day 1; experimental group) or long-course chemoradiotherapy (50·4 Gy in 28 fractions with concurrent oral capecitabine 825 mg/m2 twice daily) followed by two cycles of CAPOX (standard-of-care group). After surgery, both groups received six cycles of adjuvant CAPOX, and the experimental group additionally received adjuvant camrelizumab for up to 15 cycles. The primary endpoint was BIRC-assessed pathological complete response rate in the intention-to-treat population, which has been previously reported. Here, we performed a prespecified interim analysis of investigator-assessed event-free survival (one of the key secondary endpoints, defined as time from randomisation to radiographic progression precluding surgery, local recurrence or distant metastasis, or death) in the intention-to-treat population (all randomly assigned patients) with a boundary of a two-sided p values less than 0·0102. Safety was evaluated in all patients who received at least one dose of the study treatment according to the assigned regimen. The study was registered with ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT04928807, and is active, but no longer recruiting. FINDINGS: Between July 23, 2021, and March 1, 2023, 231 patients (153 [66%] males and 78 [34%] females; 227 [98%] were Han Chinese, and four [2%] were other ethnicity Chinese) were randomly assigned to the experimental group (n=113) and standard-of-care group (n=118). As of Oct 1, 2025, the median follow-up duration was 36·7 months (IQR 32·6-39·9) in the experimental group and 34·7 months (31·1-39·1) in the standard-of-care group. The 3-year investigator-assessed event-free survival rate was 91·3% (95% CI 83·9-95·4) in the experimental group versus 77·4% (67·9-84·4) in the standard-of-care group (stratified hazard ratio 0·33 [0·15-0·71]; two-sided log-rank p=0·0029). During the entire treatment period, the most common grade 3 or 4 treatment-related adverse events were decreased lymphocyte count (23 [20%] of 115 in the experimental group vs 31 [28%] of 112 in the standard-of-care group), decreased white blood cell count (13 [11%] vs 16 [14%]), decreased neutrophil count (13 [11%] vs 13 [12%]), and decreased platelet count (seven [6%] vs 15 [13%]). Treatment-related serious adverse events occurred in 22 (19%) versus 15 (13%) patients, with the most common being decreased platelet count (one [1%] vs six [5%]), and radiation gastroenteritis (two [2%] vs four [4%]). Treatment-related deaths occurred in one patient in the experimental group (septic shock related to chemotherapy, but unrelated to camrelizumab) and none in the standard-of-care group. INTERPRETATION: In this interim analysis, short-course radiotherapy followed by camrelizumab and CAPOX significantly improved 3-year event-free survival in patients with locally advanced rectal cancer, with a safety profile similar to long-course chemoradiotherapy followed by CAPOX. Comparison of this promising new treatment strategy with contemporary total neoadjuvant therapy strategies is warranted. FUNDING: Key Clinical Research Initiative Program of Union Hospital, National Key Technology Research and Development Programme of Hubei Province, and Jiangsu Hengrui Pharmaceuticals. TRANSLATION: For the Chinese translation of the abstract see Supplementary Materials section.

Authors: Kim DH, Jang DW, Hwang SH
Journal: Head & neck | DOI: 10.1002/hed.70524
Published: 2026-Oct-27
PMID: 42947529



Abstract:
BACKGROUND: We performed an outcome-specific network meta-analysis comparing contemporary energy devices in thyroidectomy. METHODS: Randomized controlled trials comparing conventional hemostasis with Harmonic, LigaSure, Thunderbeat, or other advanced energy devices during thyroidectomy were included. Frequentist random-effects network meta-analyses were performed per outcome, with treatments ranked by P-scores and consistency assessed via design-by-treatment interaction and node-splitting analyses. RESULTS: Compared to conventional hemostasis, Harmonic significantly reduced operative time (SMD, -1.88), blood loss (SMD, -2.29), drainage volume (SMD, -1.77), hospital stay (SMD, -0.74), transient hypocalcemia (OR, 0.61), transient recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy (OR, 0.63), and postoperative bleeding (OR, 0.56). LigaSure improved operative efficiency but showed less consistent recovery and safety benefits. Harmonic ranked highest across most outcomes. CONCLUSIONS: Harmonic showed the most favorable relative effects across the evaluated outcomes. However, these findings do not establish overall device superiority; selection should consider absolute benefits and device-specific characteristics.

item.title: #4 [0/100] Targeting Engrailed-1 Fibroblasts in Idiopathic Subglottic Stenosis.

Authors: Saeedi N, Collins SL, Lopez-Fay DC, Li YCC, Abd-Elazem I, Hillel AT, Motz KM
Journal: The Laryngoscope | DOI: 10.1002/lary.71012
Published: 2026-Oct-27
PMID: 42947382



Abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Idiopathic subglottic stenosis (iSGS) is characterized by pathologic deposition of extracellular matrix (ECM) secondary to dysregulated fibroblasts. Engrailed-1 expressing fibroblasts have been shown to promote ECM deposition in fibrosis. Verteporfin has been shown to reduce EN1 expression in fibroblasts through YAP/TAZ signaling. However, EN1 expression, YAP/TAZ signaling, and verteporfin treatment have not been investigated in iSGS pathogenesis. METHODS: Biopsies of diseased subglottis and distal healthy trachea of iSGS patients (n = 6) were assessed. qRT-PCR, analysis of iSGS single-cell RNA sequencing data, flow cytometry and immunochemistry were used to compare the expression of EN1. Fibroblasts from diseased iSGS tissue were treated with verteporfin (5 μM) or control and gene and protein expression analysis was performed for EN1, YAP/TAZ pathway and fibrotic genes. RESULTS: The iSGS subglottis demonstrated increased expression of EN1 (fold change = 58.86, SD = 65.12, p: 0.031) compared to controls. Immunohistochemistry analysis of the diseased iSGS subglottis showed that EN1 was densely expressed. Verteporfin treatment of iSGS fibroblasts in vitro led to an 81.75% (SD = 9.28, p: 0.031) reduction in COL1A1 and 22.77% (SD = 17.11, p: 0.031) reduction in COL3A1 gene expression. This was associated with a 26.32% (SD = 28.25, p: 0.031) reduction in EN1 expression and reductions in the YAP/TAZ associated genes AMOTL2, CCN1, CCN2, YAP1, and WWTR1. CONCLUSION: EN1 and the associated YAP/TAZ signaling pathway are increased in iSGS. Verteporfin treatment inhibited YAP/TAZ expression and attenuated EN1 and COL1A1 expression in vitro. Targeting EN1 expressing fibroblasts through inhibition of YAP/TAZ signaling represents a potential therapeutic target to reduce fibrosis in iSGS. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: N/A.

Authors: Kim JM, Jeon SY, Lee YC, Kim SI, Eun YG
Journal: Oral diseases | DOI: 10.1111/odi.70536
Published: 2026-Oct-27
PMID: 42946967



Abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To determine whether preoperative blood inflammatory ratios discriminate malignant from benign parotid tumours. METHODS: This retrospective single-centre study included 204 patients undergoing parotidectomy (45 malignant, 159 benign); inflammatory-index analyses included 45 malignant and 157 benign cases. The neutrophil-to-lymphocyte and monocyte-to-lymphocyte ratios were the two primary indices. Group differences were tested non-parametrically with multiplicity control, discrimination by receiver operating characteristic analysis and association by multivariable logistic regression. RESULTS: Median neutrophil-to-lymphocyte and monocyte-to-lymphocyte ratios were higher in malignant tumours (2.00 vs. 1.81 and 0.203 vs. 0.166), but effect sizes were small. Areas under the curve were 0.608 (95% confidence interval 0.518-0.701) and 0.631 (0.520-0.735), respectively. At the sample-derived neutrophil-to-lymphocyte threshold, sensitivity was 86.7% and specificity 35.7%. Additional inflammatory indices, histological subgroup analyses and sensitivity analyses did not materially improve discrimination. CONCLUSIONS: Although the two primary ratios were higher in malignant tumours, their distributions overlapped substantially and discrimination was poor. These findings do not support their use as stand-alone markers for preoperative malignancy risk stratification.

Authors: Smith GI, Petersen MC, Hartig SM, Klein S
Journal: Nature medicine | DOI: 10.1038/s41591-026-04718-7
Published: 2026-Oct-27
PMID: 42946879



Abstract:
Multi-organ-system insulin resistance is the key pathogenic driver of obesity-related metabolic complications and diseases, such as atherogenic dyslipidemia, metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease and type 2 diabetes. However, there is considerable heterogeneity in insulin sensitivity among people with obesity. Some are considered to have metabolically healthy obesity, with normal insulin sensitivity in conjunction with normal fasting blood glucose, oral glucose tolerance, plasma lipid profile and intrahepatic triglyceride content. In this Review, we discuss metabolic differences at the cellular, organ-system and systemic levels between people with metabolically healthy and metabolically unhealthy obesity; we also discuss heterogeneity in the therapeutic effects of weight reduction. A better understanding of the differences between metabolically divergent groups and the physiological responses to weight loss can help identify the factors responsible for the link between excess adiposity and metabolic dysfunction and disease.

Authors: Song Y, Li X, Wu T, Yu R, Gu D, Wang H, Liu J, Zhao Y, Ren J, Chen F
Journal: The Laryngoscope | DOI: 10.1002/lary.70987
Published: 2026-Oct-27
PMID: 42946397



Abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To establish a murine heterotopic laryngeal transplantation (LT) model with a single HLA-A2 mismatch and to develop a multidimensional framework for dynamic evaluation of immune rejection and graft injury. METHODS: Laryngeal grafts from HLA-A2 transgenic mice were transplanted into C57BL/6 recipients to generate an HLA-mismatched LT model, with syngeneic C57BL/6 → C57BL/6 transplants as controls. A multidimensional evaluation system was established, integrating physiological monitoring (survival, body weight, graft appearance, neck circumference, computed tomography, and ultrasonography), immunological profiling (histopathology, immunohistochemistry, and flow cytometry), and inflammatory assessments (cytokines and biochemical parameters) from Day 0 to 12 weeks posttransplantation. RESULTS: Compared with syngeneic transplantation, the HLA-mismatched group showed aggravated immune rejection and graft injury. Progressive graft volume reduction was an early discriminator, detectable at 1 week posttransplantation and correlating with graft surface darkening and ulceration. Immunophenotyping revealed early CD4+ and CD8+ T-cell infiltration beginning at 1 week, whereas regulatory T cells increased at 3 days before markedly declining. Cytokine profiling showed elevations of MIP-1β, G-CSF, and IL-10 from 4 weeks onward, consistent with immune activation and graft injury. CONCLUSION: A murine heterotopic LT model with an HLA-A2 mismatch was established, demonstrating that a single HLA Class I disparity was sufficient to drive progressive immune rejection and graft injury in LT. A panel of biomarkers associated with adverse graft outcomes was observed, providing indicators for monitoring HLA-driven immune injury. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: N/A.

Authors: Kreslake JM, Azadi M, McKay T, Schillo B
Journal: Preventive medicine | DOI: 10.1016/j.ypmed.2026.108686
Published: 2026-Oct-27
PMID: 42946022



Abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To assess whether e-cigarette use is associated with subsequent health symptoms over time among young people in the United States. METHODS: Logistic regression analyses of online survey data from seven waves (2020-2025, N = 5917) of a probability-based longitudinal cohort (aged 15-24 years at enrollment) tested the association between e-cigarette use duration and subsequent persistent symptoms, controlling for other tobacco use, baseline self-rated health, and demographic characteristics. E-cigarette use was defined as: none (no use at any wave); experimental (use at 1 wave); sustained (use at ≥2 waves). Symptoms were defined as persistent if reported in past-month at ≥2 waves. RESULTS: Compared with no use, sustained e-cigarette use was associated with greater odds of persistent respiratory, somatic, and oral health symptoms at later waves. Significant associations included coughing/wheezing, chest pain/tightness, shortness of breath, difficulty sleeping, rapid heartbeat, high blood pressure, nausea/vomiting, weight changes, dry mouth/throat, and change/loss of taste (ORs: 1.43-2.84). Experimental use was associated with fewer persistent symptoms, including chest congestion, weight changes, dry mouth/throat, and change/loss of taste (ORs: 1.80-3.46). CONCLUSIONS: Findings support monitoring persistent symptoms associated with e-cigarette use, independent of other tobacco use, as potential indicators of longer-term health risks.

Authors: George S, Vaishampayan U, Hutson A, Groman A, Pili R, Green K, Herbst L, Kallicharan-Smith R, DiRaddo AM, Farrell E, et al.
Journal: The Lancet. Oncology | DOI: 10.1016/S1470-2045(26)00394-3
Published: 2026-Oct-27
PMID: 42945979



Abstract:
BACKGROUND: VEGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) are considered the backbone for the treatment of metastatic clear-cell renal cell carcinoma. We hypothesise that the administration of bevacizumab during scheduled breaks in pazopanib (TKI) treatment can improve tolerability and prolong progression-free survival compared with historical controls. METHODS: In this single-arm, phase 1/2 trial in five US academic cancer centres, patients (aged ≥18 years) with histologically confirmed metastatic clear-cell renal cell carcinoma, Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status of 1 or less, and adequate organ functions were included. The phase 1 portion included patients with up to one previous therapy with high-dose IL-2 or an anti-PD-1 compound alone or in combination with a CTLA-4 inhibitor. The phase 2 portion enrolled only patients with treatment-naive metastatic clear-cell renal cell carcinoma. The primary endpoint of phase 1 was to find the recommended phase 2 dose (RP2D). We tested a novel regimen using four dose levels: oral pazopanib (600 or 800 mg daily on days 1-28, followed by a 7 day break) alternating with intravenous bevacizumab (5, 7·5, or 10 mg/kg, one on day 36 and one on day 50) on a 10-week cycle in patients with metastatic clear-cell renal cell carcinoma naive to TKI treatment. The primary endpoint of phase 2 was median progression-free survival, assessed by a masked central statistician review. Dose selection (in patients who had completed 15 weeks) and activity (in patients who had completed one full 10-week cycle of the novel regimen) were analysed in the per-protocol population. Safety analyses included all patients who received any treatment. This trial was registered with ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT01684397) and is ongoing but closed to new participants. FINDINGS: Between Nov 21, 2012, and June 11, 2018, phase 1 enrolled 25 patients, with 18 patients evaluable for dose-limiting toxicity during the extended 15-week safety assessment period. The RP2D was established as pazopanib 800 mg daily (days 1-28) and bevacizumab 10 mg/kg on days 36 and 50 of a 10-week cycle. Between Jan 23, 2019, and Oct 19, 2023, phase 2 enrolled 53 patients, of whom 51 (including six from phase 1) were evaluable for activity and 59 were evaluable for safety. 36 (71%) patients were male and 15 (29%) were female, and 48 (94%) patients were White. 33 (65%) patients in phase 2 had favourable risk per the International Metastatic Renal Cell Carcinoma Database Consortium categories. After a median follow-up of 63·7 months (IQR 16·2-73·5), median progression-free survival was 24·8 months (95% CI 17·2-34·3). The most common grade 3-4 treatment-related adverse events were hypertension (20 [34%] of 59) and elevated aspartate aminotransferase (seven [12%]) and alanine aminotransferase (ten [17%]). Five (8%) patients discontinued the study for drug-related serious adverse events. No treatment-related deaths occurred. INTERPRETATION: The phase 1 portion identified the safe RP2D. The phase 2 portion showed that this novel regimen has promising antitumour activity in patients with metastatic clear-cell renal cell carcinoma in the predominantly favourable risk group who are naive to treatment. Phase 3 randomised controlled trial data are needed to confirm these findings. FUNDING: The Roswell Park Comprehensive Cancer Center (RPCCC), US National Cancer Institute (NCI), Novartis.

item.title: #10 [0/100] Chemoradiotherapy versus radiotherapy as adjuvant treatment for head and neck adenoid cystic carcinoma: a meta-analysis.

Authors: Young TC, Yap WK, Chang KP, Lee YC, Lin CH, Cheng-En Hsieh R, Kang CJ, Fang KH, Tsai YT, Chen PY, et al.
Journal: Oral oncology | DOI: 10.1016/j.oraloncology.2026.108193
Published: 2026-Oct-27
PMID: 42945915



Abstract:
OBJECTIVES: The benefit of adding chemotherapy to postoperative radiotherapy for head and neck adenoid cystic carcinoma (ACC) remains uncertain. We compared adjuvant chemoradiotherapy (CRT) with radiotherapy (RT) alone. METHODS: PubMed, Embase, and Scopus were searched from inception through May 6, 2026, with manual reference-list checking. Comparative studies reporting time-to-event outcomes for CRT versus RT were eligible. Hazard ratios (HRs) were pooled using random-effects models with restricted maximum likelihood estimation and the Hartung-Knapp adjustment. The review was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420261485857). RESULTS: Eight studies contributed 836 outcome-specific observations. CRT was not associated with improved overall survival (six studies; 648 patients; HR, 0.99; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.70-1.41; I2 = 0%), disease-free/progression-free survival (five studies; 534 patients; HR, 1.04; 95% CI, 0.81-1.34; I2 = 0%), or distant metastasis-free survival (six studies; 574 patients; HR, 0.95; 95% CI, 0.55-1.63; I2 = 44.5%). Neither locoregional control (two studies; 354 patients; HR, 0.09; 95% CI, 0.00-59.00) nor locoregional failure-free survival (three studies; 262 patients; HR, 0.91; 95% CI, 0.32-2.60) improved significantly; both estimates were imprecise. Results were consistent in adjusted-versus-unadjusted subgroup and leave-one-out analyses. CONCLUSION: Available nonrandomized evidence does not demonstrate that adjuvant CRT improves survival compared with RT alone in head and neck ACC. Evidence for locoregional outcomes remains sparse and imprecise. These findings do not support routine chemotherapy but favor individualized treatment decisions.
